outcome: Judged: the status rests on Mantovanelli's unreviewed July 2026 preprint (arXiv:2607.04365), which claims that no odd perfect number has smallest prime divisor 5, 7, 11, 13 or 17. That is a case of the bullet, and the claim is doubtful. [Judged 2026-09-28; the researcher's original outcome follows.] The existence question remains fully open, but the constraints any odd perfect number would have to satisfy were tightened in the window by at least two peer-reviewed, non-AI results: Zelinsky's new bounds on T(n) and H(n) in terms of the smallest prime factor (submitted 22 Feb 2024, published in Integers 25 (2025) #A59), and Stone's improved upper bound depending on the number of prime divisors (Integers 24 (2024) #A114, published Dec 2024, though originally received Dec 2021 and revised Feb 2024). Several self-published 'proofs' of full nonexistence surfaced on academia.edu, ResearchGate, SSRN and Zenodo, and a 2026 preprint claims to close some small-prime branches, but none of these are digested by experts or in a venue with peer review, so none change the status beyond 'progress'.
summary: The problem (does any odd perfect number exist?) is a pure existence question, so under §3.1 no amount of narrowing the search space settles it; the correct default remains 'open'. But real, dated, peer-reviewed progress on the necessary conditions occurred in the window, which the triage's cursory pass surfaced only indirectly (it found only non-credible nonexistence claims and one unverified 2026 preprint). I read the actual PDF of Zelinsky's 'The sum of the reciprocals of the prime divisors of an odd perfect or odd primitive non-deficient number' (arXiv:2402.14234, first submitted 22 Feb 2024 — six days after the frozen revision's 26 Jan 2024 timestamp, so squarely in-window; final version published in Integers 25 (2025) #A59, received 12/10/24, accepted 5/24/25). It proves new bounds on T(n) and H(n) (functions of the reciprocal-prime-sum and abundancy-related product) in terms of the smallest prime factor of a hypothetical odd perfect number, tightening prior Cohen/Suryanarayana bounds. No AI tool of any kind is mentioned in the acknowledgements or body — the paper credits only human mathematicians (Nielsen, Eve Zelinsky, a referee, and editors) for corrections. I also confirmed via search snippet and citation record that Andrew Stone's 'Improved Upper Bounds for Odd Perfect Numbers — Part I' (Integers 24 (2024) #A114) was published in December 2024, giving new upper bounds depending on the number of distinct prime factors; this is cited by Zelinsky's paper as [26], corroborating it is a real, distinct, peer-reviewed advance. I classify the decisive dated event as Zelinsky's Feb 2024 submission since it is the earliest clearly in-window, peer-reviewed advance I verified in full; Stone's result is a second, separately-dated (also in-window, if the Feb 2024 revision date is used rather than the Dec 2021 original submission) advance, noted here rather than given its own record per the instructions. I also checked the Ochem-Rao computational-bound webpage (lirmm.fr/~ochem/opn/), which parenthetically claims the classic 10^1500 lower bound (Ochem-Rao 2012, predates the window) has since been 'pushed... to N > 10^2200', with file timestamps suggesting activity as late as February 2025 — but the page gives no clear date for when 10^2200 specifically was reached, there is no accompanying paper, and Wayback Machine access was unavailable in this environment to establish an archived timeline, so I could not verify this bound as an in-window, citable event and have excluded it from the record rather than guess a date. I found no evidence anywhere — journal papers, the Ochem-Rao site, or any of the self-published claims I checked (Mantovanelli's July 2026 arXiv preprint 2607.04365, academia.edu, ResearchGate, SSRN, Zenodo) — that any AI system was involved in this area's mathematics. The 2607.04365 preprint (single author, Marco Mantovanelli, submitted 5 Jul 2026) claims to close minimal-prime branches q=5,7,11,13,17 using 'JSONL certificate bundles, Python verifier scripts, and SHA256 hashes' — traditional computational verification, not AI, and unreviewed by experts, so even if legitimate it would only be 'claimed' status at best and doesn't change the overall picture. I disagree with the triage's implicit framing that this problem's post-window activity is dominated by dubious nonexistence claims: real incremental peer-reviewed progress (Zelinsky, Stone) exists and was findable, though it required opening full PDFs rather than relying on search snippets.
competing_reading: One could argue the status should remain 'open' rather than 'progress', on the theory that these are incremental technical bounds unlikely to interest a 'careful person' writing this bullet's one-line Wikipedia entry, which only states the existence question and the headline N > 10^1500 / nine-distinct-primes facts (both predating the window and unchanged on the live article). Since the live Wikipedia article itself has not been updated to reflect Zelinsky's or Stone's results, a stricter reading tied purely to what changed in the canonical one-line summary might prefer 'open'. I use 'progress' because §3.1 explicitly says size is not the test and a bound that moved even a little counts, and both papers are genuine, dated, peer-reviewed tightenings of necessary conditions on any hypothetical odd perfect number.
what_would_settle_it: Confirmation (e.g. via an archived snapshot of lirmm.fr/~ochem/opn/ from before 26 Jan 2024, or a dated arXiv paper) of exactly when the Ochem-Rao computational bound moved from 10^1500 to 10^2200 would let that be added as a further, likely more headline-worthy, progress event. Expert digestion or journal acceptance of Mantovanelli's 2607.04365 would upgrade that item from unverified preprint to citable partial progress.

events.credibility_reason: Single-author preprint claiming an unconditional result (e.g. no odd perfect number coprime to 3 with smallest prime 5) far beyond what is known, via a finite certificate reduction of a kind the problem has resisted; no expert uptake, though under three months have passed, too little for not_credible.

events.credibility_reason: Non-reviewed venues, no uptake on a landmark problem, record's searches found no expert engagement; record did not read them in full.

judgement.doubts: The status now rests on a doubtful, unreviewed case claim. If Mantovanelli's preprint draws no uptake or is found to be wrong, the status falls back to progress (Zelinsky/Stone bounds). The record's researcher wrongly said an unreviewed case would be 'claimed' at best (F1); under §4 it is partial. The self-published whole-problem claims are dated only loosely in the record and are set aside.
